```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_amr <- requireNamespace("AMR", quietly = TRUE)
library(opamr)
```

Prescribing and resistance data use different vocabularies for the same drug:

| Vocabulary | Example for co-amoxiclav | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| BNF chemical code | `0501013K0` | NHS prescribing data, OpenPrescribing |
| `AMR` code | `AMC` | the `AMR` package, susceptibility test results |
| ATC code | `J01CR02` | WHO, ESAC-Net, GLASS, defined daily doses |
| Name | Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid | everyone, spelled in different ways |

`opamr` translates between them with the bundled `antibiotic_crosswalk` table.

## The crosswalk table

```{r}
dim(antibiotic_crosswalk)
head(antibiotic_crosswalk[, c("bnf_chemical_code", "bnf_name", "ab", "ab_name", "atc")], 8)
```

The table has one row per BNF chemical substance. Several chemicals can map to one antimicrobial, one for
each salt or formulation:

```{r}
sys <- antibiotic_crosswalk[antibiotic_crosswalk$bnf_chapter == "05", ]
dup <- sys[sys$ab %in% sys$ab[duplicated(sys$ab)], c("ab_name", "bnf_chemical_code", "bnf_name")]
dup[order(dup$ab_name), ]
```

The same agent also appears in several BNF chapters. Chapter 5 holds systemic use (oral and injectable).
Chapters 7, 11, 12 and 13 hold vaginal, eye, ear and skin products:

```{r}
table(chapter = antibiotic_crosswalk$bnf_chapter)
```

## Converting names and codes to BNF codes

`ab_to_bnf()` accepts these inputs, and they can be mixed in one call:

```{r}
ab_to_bnf(c("AMC",                 # AMR code
            "Co-trimoxazole",      # BNF or common name
            "J01XE01",             # ATC code
            "Carbapenems"),        # AMR group
          use_amr = FALSE)[, c("input", "ab", "bnf_chemical_code", "bnf_name", "via")]
```

ATC prefixes select whole classes, following the ATC hierarchy:

```{r}
ab_to_bnf("J01C", output = "codes")    # all beta-lactam penicillins
```

### Systemic and topical scope

`ab_to_bnf()` returns only chapter 5 (systemic) codes by default. Use `scope = "all"` to include topical
and other formulations:

```{r}
ab_to_bnf("fusidic acid", output = "codes", use_amr = FALSE)
ab_to_bnf("fusidic acid", scope = "all", use_amr = FALSE)[, c("bnf_chemical_code", "bnf_name")]
```

Systemic and topical prescribing measure different exposures. Fusidic acid cream and fusidic acid tablets,
for example, are rarely interchangeable in an analysis. Keeping them apart by default stops them being
pooled by accident.

### Free text and brand names

If the `AMR` package is installed, inputs that the bundled table does not recognise are passed to
`AMR::as.ab()`. That function handles brand names, misspellings and synonyms. The `via` column records how
each input was resolved, because `AMR::as.ab()` matching is fuzzy:

```{r, eval = has_amr}
ab_to_bnf(c("Augmentin", "amoxycillin", "Macrobid"))[, c("input", "ab_name", "bnf_chemical_code", "via")]
```

If `AMR::as.ab()` picks an agent with no BNF chemical, `ab_to_bnf()` warns and names the agent, so a wrong
match is visible rather than silently returning nothing:

```{r, eval = has_amr}
x <- ab_to_bnf("amikacin")
```

Amikacin is given almost entirely in hospital, so it does not appear in community prescribing data.

## From BNF codes back to antimicrobials

`bnf_to_ab()` maps a code of any length:

- longer than 9 characters (product or presentation): truncated to the chemical substance;
- exactly 9 characters (chemical substance): looked up directly;
- shorter than 9 characters (section, paragraph, subparagraph): expanded to every crosswalk chemical in that
  part of the BNF.

```{r}
bnf_to_ab(c("0501013K0AAAJAJ", "050105"))[, c("input", "bnf_chemical_code", "ab", "ab_name")]
bnf_to_atc(c("0501013B0", "0501120L0", "0501130R0"))
```

`bnf_class()` gives the BNF paragraph name, which is a convenient class variable for prescribing data:

```{r}
bnf_class(c("0501013B0", "0501021L0", "0501050B0", "0501130R0"))
```

## Aggregating to antibiotic classes

`op_example` carries `AMR` codes, so `AMR` functions can add class information. Here the bundled
`ab_group` column is used to sum 2025 items by class:

```{r}
ex <- op_example[format(op_example$date, "%Y") == "2025", ]
grp <- antibiotic_crosswalk$ab_group[match(ex$ab, antibiotic_crosswalk$ab)]
ex$class <- sub(" \\|.*$", "", grp)                     # first AMR group of each agent
by_class <- aggregate(items ~ class, data = ex, FUN = sum)
head(by_class[order(-by_class$items), ], 8)
```

The same can be done by BNF paragraph:

```{r}
ex$bnf_class <- bnf_class(substr(ex$code, 1, 9))
head(sort(tapply(ex$items, ex$bnf_class, sum), decreasing = TRUE), 6)
```

If `AMR` is installed, its own functions add more information, for example WHO defined daily doses:

```{r, eval = has_amr}
data.frame(ab = c("AMX", "DOX", "NIT"),
           name = AMR::ab_name(c("AMX", "DOX", "NIT")),
           oral_ddd_g = AMR::ab_ddd(c("AMX", "DOX", "NIT"), administration = "oral"))
```

Converting prescribing to defined daily doses needs the strength and pack size of each presentation.
OpenPrescribing's `quantity` (tablets, ml) does not provide these on its own, so `opamr` reports items.

## How the crosswalk was built, and its limits

- **Source of BNF codes.** Distinct BNF chemical substances in the English Prescribing Dataset for December
  2025 and June 2026. Chemicals not dispensed in the community in those months are absent, such as most
  hospital-only injectables.
- **Matching.** BNF names were matched to `AMR` codes with `AMR::as.ab()` on cleaned name variants, with salt
  words removed and bracketed synonyms split. A match was kept only if the agent's first non-salt word occurs
  in the BNF name. This rule rejects false matches such as "Sodium citrate" to "Sodium aminosalicylate".
- **Manual corrections.** `data-raw/manual_overrides.csv` in the source repository holds nine hand-checked
  entries. Eight fix a mapping, for example colistimethate to colistin and plain ceftazidime rather than
  ceftazidime/avibactam. One records that rifampicin combined preparations have no single `AMR` agent, so they
  are left out of the table.
- **Scope.** Antibacterials (including antimycobacterials), antifungals and topical anti-infectives.
  Antivirals and antiparasitics are left out because the `AMR` package keeps them in separate datasets.
- **Versions.** Built with `AMR` `r unique(antibiotic_crosswalk$amr_version)`. Run
  `data-raw/build_crosswalk.R` again after an `AMR` update or a BNF change.

```{r}
table(antibiotic_crosswalk$match_method)
```
